cards.title: Upcoming critical PHP security release

depth.text: PHP is preparing a **security release** for **two critical vulnerabilities**, and users should update quickly

The release is scheduled for **Wednesday, 21 October 2026 at 14:00 UTC**; PHP says it may come earlier if either vulnerability’s details become public or there is evidence of active exploitation. Commenters say an **exploit is already out**.

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters recommend shutting sites or servers down until the patch; others suggest temporary mitigations, such as blocking requests or turning off session upload progress.

comments.text: For everyone wondering why the patch is not out yet: There are a handful people responsible for doing a release. They are still asleep. To be honest, I am also shocked, that the exploit was published that quickly, after the leaked video (which was the reason, why the announcement happened in the first place, at that specific time). We expected a bit more time, even with LLMs...

The exploit is already out. Yeah this looks like it's going to go on history as the worst vulnerability ever. And now with LLMs you'll likely see tens of thousands of agents hacking any php website out there within hours.
I tried it on a personal site, was able to dump the entire database. Immediately shut all my sites down. This is bad.

If the rumors for these exploits being shared on Twitter are correct this is going to be a nightmare. I wouldn't be surprised if VPS hosts step in to mitigate it somehow since so many cheap/unmaintained LAMP installs are running on those servers.

Two things you can do now: 1. Turn off session upload progress 2. Block multipart requests at the web server More info:
https://www.vincentschmalbach.com/cve-2026-109618-and-cve-20...

cards.title: What shall I teach my son?

depth.text: a programmer expecting his first child wonders **what to teach** as **programming feels less valuable**

He points out that schools survived the radio, motion pictures, and the internet, then offers **new purposes** for education, including making tools and narratives that make us. He wants to **work out education’s purpose** with his son.

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters emphasize values, curiosity, and adaptability; others say school is mainly childcare or doesn’t prepare students well for life and work.

cards.title: Sixteen years after Deepwater Horizon, deep sea life shows few signs of recovery

depth.text: deep-sea life in the Gulf still shows **few signs of recovery** sixteen years after the **Deepwater Horizon** spill

A study found populations of octopus, squid, krill, shrimp, and lanternfish declined by **at least 60 percent** in the first few years after the 2010 disaster, with little evidence they had bounced back. Researchers called the spill “the most parsimonious explanation,” but **stopped short of concluding** it caused the declines.

entities: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

comments.text: The Deepwater disaster recovery very effectively demonstrated the phenomenon of "out of sight out of mind". they dumped almost 2 million gallons of "dispersants" on the oil spill... which was DESIGNED to make the oil heavier than water and sink to the sea bed. it never dissolved anything, it just hid the problem from the public. and all that oil is just sitting on the sea bed.
Interesting that the spill hasn't dampened long term prospects for offshore drilling (besides the brief push against it around 2016) whereas Chernobyl basically nerfed American nuclear power gen.

> While researchers stopped short of concluding that the oil spill had caused the declines Why though? Why are we so afraid of accountability? Because this is what people point to when trying to deny things are true: ThErE iS NO EviDeNce, sHoW Me THe StUdY, etc. etc.

And the companies are also struggling to recover, right? Because the damage to the company is commensurate with the damage to the environment it works within? No? The companies are largely free from consequence? Maybe our system is a bit broken.

cards.title: My Friend Bob Cringely

depth.text: someone remembers **Bob Cringely** as a charming friend who kept chasing **startup ideas**

Tyma and Cringely first worked together on **Pronto**, which downloaded magazine PDFs over idle internet connections and printed them at home overnight. Later, Cringely turned Tyma’s email about **C# and Java** into a lightly edited blog post; the two then went to Sun Microsystems, where executives defended Java and gave Tyma **nasty looks**.

cards.camps: Two camps: most readers praise the warm tribute; one says it comes across as “damning with faint praise.”

comments.text: Mark Stephens (aka Robert X. Cringely) obituary: https://www.hillandwood.com/obituaries/Mark-Stephens?obId=49... Very entertaining.)

Paul Tyma - 3 posts in 20 years. A prolific blogger! :)

cards.title: Academics have a duty to defend open knowledge systems like Wikipedia

depth.text: the post argues academics should help defend **open knowledge systems** like **Wikipedia**

One commenter says universities should recognize **Wikipedia contributions** as public service and provide support; critics warn that citations can be **gamed** or become useless if cited content disappears. Another commenter suggests AI companies send **5% of revenue** to support Wikipedia and researchers.

cards.camps: Two camps: supporters want universities to recognize Wikipedia contributions; critics say citations and open editing can spread unreliable or manipulated information.

cards.title: 2026 is an exciting year for the Rust compiler (and me)

depth.text: someone says **years of Rust compiler work** are finally unlocking **faster builds** and **long-awaited features**

The **next-generation trait solver**, in the works for **almost 10 years** in various forms, fixes soundness bugs and unblocks features; Polonius enables more code to compile. The post also calls LLVM 23 an unexpectedly large performance win, while Cargo sharing artifacts between cargo check and cargo build could shrink the target directory by **5-30%**, depending on the workload.

cards.camps: Two camps: one commenter says Rust's spread has hurt compile times and it isn't the future; others are excited about compiler progress and hope for improvements.

comments.text: I don't think rust is the future anymore, despite having contributed to its compiler few times and been quite involved for years. It has spread too much and that impact compiles time too much. I think a newer language, having the boreness of go, the compile speed and maybe comp time of zig and safety of rust will emerge, maybe with lisp syntax.

> It's easy to understate how big of a deal this is for the compiler. This work resolves a major piece of technical debt that a lot of compiler developers dreamed about for years. No kidding. I’ve been waiting for the solver at least half that decade now. Hopefully it and Polonius unblock specialization which has been in purgatory for years.
Smaller target directory size would be such a lifesaver. Hoping the best for you, and Rust!

I'm curious about polymorphism. Should it be default on for debug builds just to save storage and compile time? How will rust decide whether to enable polymorphism? Will it be possible to provide source-level polymorphism hints to the compiler?

It follows the manual’s **parts, hardware counts, and order**, with the original instructions beside the model. Panel thickness, hole positions, and shelf heights are **close estimates** read from drawings; commenters say the cam locks are on the wrong side of shelves.

glossary.CVSS: Common Vulnerability Scoring System: a scale people use to rate how serious a security flaw is.
glossary.proof of concept: A small test or demo that shows whether an idea can work.
glossary.multipart request: A web request that can carry files and other form fields together.
glossary.session upload progress: A PHP feature that tracks how much of a file upload has finished.
glossary.VPS: Virtual Private Server: a computer you rent and leave online to run your own software.
glossary.LAMP: Linux, Apache, MySQL, PHP: a common set of tools used together to run a website.
glossary.AGI: Artificial General Intelligence: a hypothetical AI that could handle many kinds of tasks, not just one narrow job.
glossary.MOOCs: Massive Open Online Courses: online classes designed for lots of people to take.
glossary.Lindy Effect: The idea that, for things that can keep going, having lasted a long time may be a sign they’ll last longer.
glossary.endowments: Money or property given to an institution to help support its work over time.
glossary.AI agent: An autonomous computer program that can carry out tasks.
glossary.tool loop: A repeating process where an AI uses a tool, checks what happened, and decides what to do next.
glossary.acoustic surveys: A way to estimate what lives underwater by using sound.
glossary.genetic diversity: The range of inherited traits found among members of a group.
glossary.parsimonious explanation: An explanation that accounts for what happened with the fewest extra assumptions.
glossary.dispersants: Chemicals used to break up oil slicks.
glossary.daemon: A program that runs in the background and handles a task without being started each time.
glossary.PDF: Portable Document Format: a file type that keeps a document’s pages laid out the same when opened or printed.
glossary.JVM: Java Virtual Machine: software that runs programs built for Java's runtime.
glossary.product-market fit: When enough customers want a product for it to work as a business.
glossary.citogenesis: A claim gets copied between sources until later writers treat those sources as proof.
glossary.WAF: Web Application Firewall: a website’s guard that checks incoming requests and can block suspicious ones.
glossary.trait solver: The part of Rust that checks whether code has the behavior it needs available.
glossary.Polonius: A newer way for Rust to check whether code uses shared data safely.
glossary.soundness bug: A flaw that lets proof-checking software accept a false result.
glossary.LLVM: A set of tools that helps turn source code into instructions a computer can run.
glossary.artifacts: Files a build creates and saves for later use.
glossary.cam lock: A fitting you turn to pull two furniture panels tight together.
glossary.cam screw: A screw whose head fits into a cam lock, so turning the lock pulls panels together.
glossary.dowel: A small wooden peg used to line up furniture pieces.
glossary.racking: When a bookcase shifts out of its square shape instead of staying straight.
glossary.IPO: Initial Public Offering: when a company first offers its shares for the public to buy.
glossary.equity: Ownership in a company, rather than lending it money.
glossary.trust: A legal arrangement where people are put in charge of managing something under agreed rules.
